title: Medication Administration (5 Rights)
summary: Safely administering medications using the 5 rights framework across all routes.
equipment: Administration supplies per route (oral cup, syringe, IV tubing, etc.)
steps: Right Patient: Verify using two identifiers (name + DOB or MRN) — ask patient to state their name.
Right Medication: Compare the medication label to the MAR — three times (pulling, preparing, administering).
Right Dose: Calculate and verify dose. Use a second nurse check for high-alert medications.
Right Route: Confirm the ordered route (PO, IV, IM, SQ, topical, etc.).
Right Time: Administer within 30 minutes before or after scheduled time (per facility policy).
Perform hand hygiene and prepare medication in a clean area.
Educate the patient on what the medication is and why it's being given.
Administer the medication per the correct route technique.
Stay with patient for PO medications until swallowed.
Document administration immediately in the MAR.
Monitor for therapeutic effects and adverse reactions per medication.
nursing_considerations: Also apply Right Reason and Right Documentation (7 Rights extended framework).
High-alert medications (insulin, heparin, opioids) require independent double-checks.
Never crush enteric-coated or extended-release medications.
Reassess patient's condition before administering — hold if contraindicated and notify provider.
Document any refused or held medications and clinical rationale.

title: Subcutaneous (SQ/SC) Injection
summary: Administering medication into the subcutaneous tissue using a short needle.
equipment: Medication in syringe (drawn up per order)
steps: Verify 5 rights. Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Select injection site: abdomen (2 inches from umbilicus), outer thigh, upper outer arm, or upper back. Rotate sites systematically.
For insulin: abdomen provides fastest/most consistent absorption; thigh slowest.
Clean site with alcohol swab in circular motion. Allow to dry completely (30 seconds).
Pinch up a fold of subcutaneous tissue with non-dominant hand.
Insert needle at 45° (thin patient or short needle) or 90° angle (average to heavy patient with ≥1 inch of subcutaneous tissue). Insert at 90° for insulin pens.
Release the skin fold once needle is inserted.
Do NOT aspirate before injecting SQ medications — aspiration is no longer recommended for any SQ injection.
Inject medication slowly and steadily.
Withdraw needle at the same angle as insertion. Apply gentle pressure with gauze — do not rub (rubbing disperses medication and causes bruising).
Dispose of needle immediately in sharps container — do NOT recap.
Document site, time, dose, and patient response.
nursing_considerations: Rotate injection sites consistently — injecting repeatedly into the same spot causes lipohypertrophy (fatty lumps) which impairs absorption.
Insulin should reach room temperature before injection — cold insulin stings and may alter absorption.
Heparin injections: apply pressure 1–2 min after but do NOT rub — rubbing causes hematomas.
Enoxaparin (Lovenox) pre-filled syringes: do NOT expel the air bubble before injection — it helps seal the drug in subcutaneous tissue.
If blood appears in syringe barrel, withdraw, discard, and prepare a new dose.

title: Intramuscular (IM) Injection
summary: Administering medication deep into muscle tissue for rapid absorption.
equipment: 20–25g, 1–3 inch needle (size based on patient and site)
steps: Verify 5 rights. Select appropriate site and needle length based on patient muscle mass and body habitus.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Select site (preference order): Ventrogluteal → Vastus lateralis → Deltoid.
Ventrogluteal: Locate the greater trochanter with your palm. Point fingers toward the patient's head. The space between index and middle finger is the injection site. Use 1.5–2 inch needle.
Deltoid: 3 finger-widths below the acromion process, on the lateral aspect. Limit to ≤1 mL. Use 1–1.5 inch needle.
Vastus lateralis: Middle third of outer thigh. Use 1–1.5 inch needle.
Dorsogluteal: NOT recommended — risk of sciatic nerve injury.
Clean site with alcohol swab. Allow to dry.
Spread or bunch skin (spread technique most common). Insert needle at 90° with a smooth, quick motion.
Inject medication steadily (10 seconds per mL).
Withdraw needle at 90°. Apply gentle pressure with gauze.
Do NOT massage — disperses medication, increases discomfort.
Dispose of needle immediately in sharps container.
Document site, dose, time, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Maximum volumes per site: deltoid 1 mL, vastus lateralis 1–3 mL, ventrogluteal up to 3–5 mL.
Ventrogluteal is the preferred site — furthest from major nerves and blood vessels, reliable muscle depth.
Avoid dorsogluteal (buttocks) — high risk of sciatic nerve damage and inconsistent muscle depth.
Z-track technique is recommended for irritating medications (iron dextran, hydroxyzine): pull skin 1–1.5 inches laterally before injecting, hold during/after, release after needle withdrawal.
Aspiration before IM injection is no longer routinely recommended — evidence does not support routine aspiration for most IM sites.

title: IV Push (IVP) Medication Administration
summary: Administering a medication directly into the bloodstream via IV access over a short defined time.
steps: Verify 5 rights. Review safe IVP push rate for the specific medication (refer to pharmacy or drug guide).
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Assess IV site for patency: no redness, swelling, or tenderness.
Clean IV access port (needleless connector or cap) with alcohol swab using friction for 15 seconds. Allow to dry.
Flush IV with 10 mL NS using push-pause technique to confirm patency. Note ease of flush and patient response.
Stop any infusing IV fluid or clamp primary line if medication is incompatible.
Connect medication syringe to the port. Inject at the prescribed rate (refer to push rate).
Many medications specify a per-minute rate: e.g., morphine 2–5 mg over 5 minutes = 1 mg per minute.
Observe patient throughout administration for adverse reactions.
After medication, flush with 10 mL NS using push-pause technique to ensure all medication clears the tubing.
Resume previous IV infusion if applicable.
Document medication, dose, time, push rate, and patient response.
nursing_considerations: Never push medications faster than the recommended rate — rapid administration of many drugs causes serious adverse effects (e.g., phenytoin cardiac dysrhythmia, furosemide ototoxicity).
High-alert IVP medications (opioids, benzodiazepines, heparin, insulin) require independent double-check.
If patient reports pain, burning, or you feel resistance during flush — stop and reassess IV patency.
Avoid giving IVP medications through small peripheral IVs (24g) or into a port that has been sluggish.
Some medications require dilution before IVP (e.g., potassium chloride is NEVER given undiluted IV push — fatal).

title: Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) Management
summary: Setting up, monitoring, and troubleshooting a PCA pump for patient-controlled opioid analgesia.
steps: Verify complete PCA order: medication, concentration, demand dose, lockout interval, 1-hour and 4-hour limit, and basal rate (if ordered).
Perform two-nurse independent double-check before programming — verify drug, concentration, dose, lockout interval, and limit settings.
Load PCA cassette into pump. Attach PCA-specific tubing (anti-siphon and anti-reflux valves required).
Connect PCA tubing to patient's IV access. Ensure IV is patent.
Program pump per verified order. Second nurse confirms all settings.
Educate patient on PCA use: press the button only when pain occurs; do NOT allow others (family) to press the button for the patient.
Ensure call light is within reach. Ensure naloxone is accessible at bedside.
Assess pain level, respiratory rate, sedation score (RASS or Pasero), SpO2 per facility protocol (commonly every 1–2 hours).
Document PCA readings every shift: total doses attempted, doses delivered, cumulative drug volume used.
If sedation score is ≥3 (on Pasero scale) or respiratory rate <10, stop PCA, stimulate patient, call for help, and administer naloxone per protocol.
Resolve PCA alarms promptly. Document all interventions.
nursing_considerations: Only the PATIENT should press the PCA button — family-assisted dosing (proxy dosing) bypasses the safety mechanism and can cause overdose.
Respiratory depression is the most serious PCA complication — monitor sedation level alongside respiratory rate; sedation precedes respiratory depression.
Basal rates are controversial — they increase risk of respiratory depression overnight in opioid-naive patients.
Monitor for constipation, urinary retention, nausea — common opioid side effects requiring management.
Waste any remaining opioid at end of shift with a witness. Document wastage.
